Contro} of Breathing (Ventilation)
The automatic control of breathing is coordinated by a respiratory centre located in the medulla oblongata
of the brainstem. This centre continuously regulates the rate and depth of ventilation to maintain homeostasis.
e The ventral portion of the medullary centre functions as the inspiratory centre. It sends rhythmic
impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles to initiate and deepen inspiration.
¢ The dorsal aid lateral portions serve as the expiratory centre, which inhibits inspiration and promotes
expiration, particularly during forceful breathing.
Together, these centres adjust ventilation in response to the body’s metabolic demands, ensuring that
oxygen uptake and carbon dioxide removal are balanced.

Voluntary and Higher Brain Control

While breathing is primarily involuntary, it can be consciously overridden via the cerebral cortex. This allows

individuals to:

e Alter the rate and depth of breathing (e.g., during speech, singing, or exercise).

© Voluntarily hold their breath—for example, during swimming or moments of concentration.

However, breath-holding is limited by rising carbon dioxide levels and falling oxygen levels in the blood. If
oxygen levels fall too low, unconsciousness occurs, and automatic breathing resumes under the control of

the respiratory centre.
Emotional Influence: The Limbic System

Breathing patterns can also be modified by emotional stimuli, which act through the limbic system—a
complex network in the brain associated with emotions and behavior. For example:

Anxiety may cause rapid, shallow breathing.

e Fear or excitement may accelerate breathing rate.

® Calmness can slow breathing.

ROLE OF RESPIRATORY PIGMENTS

Respiratory pigments are coloured molecules that play a vital role in the transport of oxygen within
organisms. These pigments bind reversibly with oxygen, allowing them to pick up oxygen in regions of high
concentration (e.g., lungs or gills) and release it where it is needed (e.g., tissues undergoing respiration). A
common feature among all respiratory pigments is the presence of a coloured, non-protein component—for
example, the haem group in haemoglobin.

Two of the most studied respiratory pigments in vertebrates are haemoglobin and myoglobin.
Haemoglobin

Haemoglobin is a large, globular protein found within red blood cells. It is composed of :our polypeptide
chains, each associated with a haem group that contains a central iron (Fe**) atom. This iron atom is capable of
binding one molecule of oxygen, allowing each haemoglobin molecule to carry up to four oxygen molecules.

Oxygen binding to haemoglobin is reversible and depends on the partial pressure of oxygen (pO,). In

oxygen-rich environments such as the alveoli of the lungs, haemoglobin readily binds oxygen to form
oxyhaemoglobin. In tissues with low pO2, oxygen is released to support cellular respiration.

S$ studyplusplus.com $

Myoglobin

Myoglobin is a structurally simpler pigment found in skeletal and cardiac muscles. It consists of a single
polypeptide chain and a single haem group, allowing it to bind one molecule of oxygen. Myoglobin has a higher
affinity for oxygen than haemoglobin and serves as an intracellular oxygen reservoir.

This pigment becomes particularly important when oxygen levels drop below 20 mmHg—a condition that
may occur during intense muscular activity. At such low oxygen pressures, myoglobin releases its stored oxygen,
thereby sustaining aerobic respiration in muscle cells when haemoglobin-derived oxygen becomes limited. It is

also responsible for the red colour of muscle tissue.

EFFECTS OF SMOKING ON THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM

Smoking is one of the most harmful lifestyle habits and a leading cause of respiratory illness worldwide.

Tobacco smoke contains thousands of toxic substances such as nicotine, tar, and carbon monoxide, along with
many cancer-causing chemicals. These substances damage the air passages, alveoli, and protective mechanisms
of the lungs, producing both short-term irritation and long-term chronic diseases.

>»

Irritation and Inflammation of Airways

When a person inhales cigarette smoke, the chemicals
irritate the lining of the trachea and bronchi. This
leads to swelling and inflammation of the airways,
accompanied by excessive mucus secretion. Over
time, this constant irritation causes a persistent
cough, often referred to as a “smoker's cough,” which
is one of the earliest warning signs of lung damage.
Paralysis of Cilia

The respiratory tract is normally lined with tiny hair-
like structures called cilia, which move rhythmically to
sweep out dust, microbes, and mucus. Smoking a
paralyzes or even destroys these cilia. As a result,

harmful particles remain trapped in the lungs instead
of being cleared out. This greatly increases the risk of
respiratory infections such as bronchitis and =
pneumonia, since the lungs lose their natural defense
system.

> Chronic Bronchitis

With long-term smoking, the bronchi remain chronically inflamed and produce large amounts of thick
mucus. The narrowed and clogged airways make breathing difficult and cause constant coughing. This
condition, known as chronic bronchitis, is commonly seen in long-term smokers who experience frequent
chest infections and reduced lung efficiency.

> Emphysema

One of the most serious effects of smoking is emphysema, in which the walls of the alveoli (air sacs) are
progressively destroyed. Instead of many small alveoli providing a large surface area for gas exchange, the
alveoli fuse into larger, less efficient sacs. This reduces the surface area for oxygen absorption, leading to
severe shortness of breath. Patients with emphysema often develop a “barrel-shaped chest” and may
become dependent on supplemental oxygen in advanced stages.

>» Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)

Chronic bronchitis and emphysema together are referred to as Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
(COPD). Smoking is the leading cause of COPD worldwide. It is a progressive disease in which airflow
becomes permanently obstructed, making exhalation difficult. Patients with COPD suffer from constant
breathlessness, wheezing, and greatly reduced exercise tolerance.

> Lung Cancer

Smoking is the major cause of lung cancer, responsible for over 80% of cases globally. Carcinogens present

in tobacco smoke damage the DNA of lung cells, leading to uncontrolled cell growth. Lung cancer is

particularly dangerous because symptoms often appear late, when the disease has already spread. This
makes survival rates very low compared to many other cancers.
>» Reduced Oxygen Transport

Another harmful effect of smoking is reduced oxygen transport in the blood. Carbon monoxide, a poisonous

gas in cigarette smoke, binds to hemoglobin with much greater affinity than oxygen. This prevents

hemoglobin from carrying oxygen efficiently, depriving tissues of oxygen. Smokers may experience fatigue,
dizziness, and a higher risk of heart and brain complications due to reduced oxygen supply.
> Increased Susceptibility to Infections

Since smoking damages both the cilia and the immune defenses of the respiratory system, smokers are far

more prone to infections such as tuberculosis, influenza, and pneumonia. Healing of damaged respiratory

tissues is also slower in smokers, further worsening recovery from illness.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), tobacco use kills more than 8 million people every year,
with respiratory diseases being a major cause of death. In countries like Pakistan, smoking-related illnesses such
as COPD, lung cancer, and tuberculosis place a heavy burden on public health systems. Many of these conditions
are preventable if smoking is avoided or stopped early in life.

Smoking affects the respiratory system by irritating and inflaming the airways, paralyzing cilia, causing
chronic bronchitis, damaging alveoli in emphysema, leading to COPD, and greatly increasing the risk of lung cancer.
It also reduces oxygen transport due to carbon monoxide and makes the body more vulnerable to infections.

Metabolic activities within body cells generate a range of waste products, many of which can become
harmful if allowed to accumulate. To prevent toxicity, these wastes must be efficiently removed. Body fluids such
as blood and lymph serve as transport mediums, carrying waste materials away from active tissues to excretory
organs.

Different systems play distinct roles in excretion. The respiratory system eliminates carbon dioxide, a major
waste product of cellular respiration, from the bloodstream. The urinary system is responsible for filtering blood
to remove nitrogenous wastes (such as urea), excess salts, and water.

In addition to excretion, the urinary system performs several vital regulatory functions. It maintains the
osmotic balance of body fluids by adjusting water and electrolyte concentrations, regulates blood pH and fluid
volume, and contributes to the control of blood pressure and red blood cell production through the secretion of
hormones like renin and erythropoietin.

NITROGENOUS COMPOUNDS EXCRETED DURING EXCRETION.

The breakdown of proteins and nucleic acids in the body produces nitrogenous wastes. These substances
are toxic if allowed to accumulate, so they must be removed efficiently through the process of excretion. The main
nitrogenous compounds excreted by humans include urea, uric acid, creatinine, and small amounts of ammonia.
Each of these compounds originates from different metabolic processes and is eliminated mainly through urine.

1. Urea

Urea is the primary nitrogenous waste in humans. It is formed in the liver through the urea cycle, where
ammonia (a highly toxic by-product of protein breakdown) is converted into a less toxic, water-soluble form.
Urea is then transported by the blood to the kidneys and excreted in urine. On average, about 80-90% of
the nitrogen excreted from the body is in the form of urea. For example, after eating a protein-rich meal,
urea levels in the blood and urine rise because more amino acids are broken down.

2. Uric Acid

Uric acid is produced during the breakdown of nucleic acids (DNA and RNA). It is less soluble in water
compared to urea. Normally, only a small quantity of uric acid is excreted in urine, but if its concentration
becomes too high, it can crystallize and deposit in joints, causing a painful disorder called gout. Birds and
reptiles excrete uric acid as their main nitrogenous waste, which conserves water since it is eliminated as a
paste-like substance.

3. Creatinine

Creatinine is formed in musc'es as a by-product of the breakdown of creatine phosphate, a compound that
stores energy for muscle contractions. It is produced at a relatively constant rate, depending on muscle
activity and mass. Because the kidneys efficiently filter creatinine from the blood, measuring its level in urine
or blood is an important clinical test of kidney function. Elevated creatinine levels may indicate impaired
kidney performance.

4. Ammonia

Ammonia is a direct by-product of amino acid metabolism. It is extremely toxic and must be removed quickly
from the body. In humans, most ammonia is converted into urea in the liver before excretion. However,
small amounts of free ammonia are excreted directly into urine, where they also help maintain the acid—
base balance of the body.

5. Other Nitrogenous Compounds

In addition to the main wastes, trace amounts of other nitrogen-containing substances such as amino acids,

peptides, and nitrogenous bases may also appear in urine. Their presence in significant amounts, however,

can be a sign of metabolic or renal disorders. For instance, excessive amino acids in urine (aminoaciduria)
may indicate defects in amino acid metabolism.

Doctors often perform a urinalysis to measure nitrogenous waste levels. For example, the blood urea
nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine test are routinely used to evaluate kidney health. Elevated levels of urea or
creatinine in blood may signal kidney disease, dehydration, or other metabolic problems. The nitrogenous
compounds excreted during excretion include urea (major form), uric acid, creatinine, and small amounts of
ammonia. Together, these wastes help the body maintain chemical balance and prevent toxic buildup. “

EXCRETORY PRODUCTS AND THEIR RELATION TO HABITATS

Different animals excrete nitrogenous wastes in forms that reflect both their metabolism and the availability
of water in their environment. The three main types of excretory products are ammonia, urea, and uric acid, and
each type is associated with particular habitats and survival strategies. This adaptation ensures that organisms
can efficiently remove toxic wastes while conserving water and energy.

1. Ammonotelic Animals: Ammonia Excretion

Ammonia is the most primitive and highly toxic nitrogenous waste. Because it is very soluble in water, it

must be excreted quickly and ina diluted form. Therefore, animals that live in aquatic habitats, where water

is abundantly available, usually excrete ammonia. To safely excrete just one gram of nitrogen as ammonia,
an organism requires approximately 500 mL of water, making this strategy feasible only for organisms in
water-rich environments.

¢ Examples: Many freshwater invertebrates and vertebrates, such as protozoans, sponges, cnidarians,

echinoderms, crustaceans, and most bony fishes, amphibians, and aquatic animals, adopt this method
of excretion. These organisms are termed ammonotelic.

Where do you think the carbon dioxide used in the formation of urea comes from? Where
does the remainder of excess carbon dioxide go to be excreted?

The carbon dioxide involved in urea formation comes from cellular respiration. Inside the
mitochondria of body cells carbohydrates, fats, and proteins are broken down to produce
energy (ATP). A majo; :-y-product of this process is carbon dioxide (C02).

In the urea cycle (whic. mainly takes place in the liver), some of this CO2 combines with
ammonia (NHs) to form carbamoyl phosphate, which then enters the cycle and eventually
contributes to the production of urea: Urea is later excreted in urine.

The remainder of the excess CO2, which is not used in the urea cycle, does not stay in the liver.
Instead, it dissolves in the blood, is carried to the lungs (mainly as bicarbonate fons, HCOs*),

and is exhaled during breathing.

STRUCTURE OF THE KIDNEY

The kidneys are the primary excretory organs of humans, responsible for filtering blood, maintaining water

and electrolyte balance, and excreting nitrogenous wastes. Each kidney is a highly specialized organ with a
complex structure that supports these vital functions. Understanding the structure of the kidney is crucial for
appreciating how it performs its role in excretion and homeostasis.

1.

External Structure
Shape, Size, and Location:

Each kidney is bean-shaped, reddish-brown in color, and measures about 10-12 cm in length, 5-7 cm in
width, and 3-4 cm in thickness in adults. They weigh approximately 120-150 grams each. The kidneys are
located in the posterior abdominal cavity on either side of the vertebral column, just below the ribcage. The
right kidney is usually slightly lower than the left due to the presence of the liver.

Hilum and Renal Capsule:

On the inner (medial) surface of each kidney is a vertical depression called the hilum. Through the hilum,
the renal artery enters, and the renal vein and ureter exit. The entire kidney is enclosed in a tough fibrous
capsule called the renal capsule, which provides protection against physical trauma and infections.
Surrounding this capsule is a layer of adipose (fatty) tissue, known as the perirenal fat, which cushions and
holds the kidney in place.
Internal Structure
When cut longitudinally, the kidney reveals three distinct regions: renal cortex, renal medulla, and renal
pelvis.
(a) Renal Cortex:
The outermost region is called the renal cortex, which appears granular due to the presence of
numerous renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules of nephrons. This is the site where blood filtration
begins.
(b) Renal Medulla:
Beneath the cortex lies the renal medulla, a-darker, striated region arranged into renal pyramids. Each
pyramid is cone-shaped, with its broad base facing the cortex and its tip (called renal papilla) projecting
into minor calyces. The striated appearance is due to the presence of loops of Henle and collecting ducts
running parallel.
(c) Renal Pelvis:
At the innermost part of the kidney lies a funnel-shaped chamber called the renal pelvis. It collects urine
from the calyces and narrows down to form the ureter, which carries urine to the bladder.
©  Calyces (minor and major): The renal papillae drain urine into small cup-like cavities called minor
calyces. These join to form major calyces, which then open into the renal pelvis.

The nephron is.the microscopic structural and functional unit of the kidney. Each kidney contains about 1—

Blood Supply of the Kidney
The kidney is richly supplied with blood, receiving about 20-25% of cardiac output. Blood enters through
the renal artery, which branches into smaller arterioles leading to the glomerulus. After filtration, blood

The kidneys are protected by multiple layers:
1. Renal capsule — tough fibrous layer directly covering the kidney.
2. Perirenal fat — cushions the organ.
3. Renal fascia — connective tissue anchoring the kidneys to surrounding structures.
These ensure the kidney remains securely in place and safe from mechanical shocks.

STRUCTURE OF A NEPHRON

The nephron is the fundamental structural and functional unit of the kidney, responsible for the filtration of
blood and the formation of urine. Each human kidney contains approximately 1 to 1.5 million nephrons, which
operate collectively to maintain fluid and electrolyte balance, remove waste products, and regulate blood pH.
Structure of the Nephron

Atypical nephron consists of two main parts:

e Renal corpuscle

¢ Renal tubule
1. Renal Corpuscle

The renal corpuscle is located in the renal cortex and is the site of initial blood filtration. It comprises:

* Glomerulus — A dense, tuft-like network of capillaries that receives blood from the afferent arteriole.

* Bowman’s capsule — A double-walled, cup-like structure that encases the glomerulus. It marks the

beginning of the renal tubule and collects the filtrate from the glomerular capillaries.
2. Renal Tubule and Associated Structures

After the filtrate is collected in Bowman's capsule, it passes through a series of specialized tubules where

selective reabsorption and secretion occur:

a. Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT)

Immediately following Bowman’s capsule, the filtrate enters the proximal convoluted tubule, a highly
coiled segment located in the cortex. This region is responsible for the reabsorption of water, ions,
glucose, and amino acids into the surrounding capillaries.

b. Loop of Henle

The PCT descends into the renal medulla to form the loop of Henle, which has two distinct limbs:

© Descending limb — Permeable to water, facilitating water reabsorption.

© Ascending limb — impermeable to water but actively transports salts out of the filtrate.

This arrangement enables the kidney to concentrate urine through the countercurrent multiplier mechanism.
¢. Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT)

As the loop of Henle ascends back toward the cortex, it transitions into the distal convoluted tubule,

another coiled segment. The DCT fine-tunes ion concentration and contributes to acid-base balance and

secretion of certain wastes.

URINE FORMATION

Urine formation in the nephron is a highly coordinated process that ensures the removal of metabolic wastes
and the regulation of blood composition. It involves three main stages:
1. Glomerular Filtration 2. Tubular Reabsorption 3. Tubular Secretion
1. Glomerular Filtration (Ultrafiltration under Pressure)
Location: Renal corpuscle (Glomerulus + Bowman's capsule)
Mechanism: Passive filtration under pressure
Glomerular filtration is the first step in urine formation. It occurs in the Bowman's capsule, where blood
from the afferent arteriole enters a bundle of capillaries known as the glomerulus.
» Hydrostatic Pressure Drives Filtration
Filtration occurs due to high hydrostatic pressure, which is generated by the incoming blood. This pressure
is unusually high in the glomerulus—significantly higher than in other capillary beds of the body.
This is achieved because the efferent arteriole (outgoing) is narrower than the afferent arteriole (incoming).
As blood is forced into a narrower vessel, pressure builds up, pushing plasma and small solutes out of the
capillaries and into the Bowman’s capsule.

There are two types of nephrons, cortical nephrons and juxtamedullary nephrons. Cortical nephrons
are found in the cortex. They have their renal corpuscle in the superficial renal cortex and have
relatively short loops of Henle. 70 to 80% nephrons in human kidney are cortical. Under normal
conditions of water availability, the cortical nephrons deal with the control of blood volume by
forming diluted urine. Juxtamedullary nephrons have their renal corpuscle close to the junction of the
cortex and medulla. They have long loop of Henle which extends deep into the medulla. These types
of nephrons are relatively rare and only comprise 20-30% of the nephrons in the human kidney. When
water is in short supply, increased water retention occurs through juxtamedullary nephrons.

Mechanism of Urine Concentration: The Countercurrent Multiplier System

The kidneys must conserve water when the body is dehydrated and remove excess water when it is
overhydrated. The ability to produce concentrated (hypertonic) urine is essential for water balance and survival
in terrestrial environments. 2

This is made possible by a specialized mechanism called the countercurrent multiplier, which operates in
the loop of Henle and is supported by the vasa recta—the capillary network surrounding the nephron.

Role of the Loop of Henle and the Vasa Recta

The loop of Henle plays a.central role in creating a gradient of solute concentration in the kidney medulla.
The descending and ascending limbs of the loop differ in their permeability:

¢. Descending limb: Permeable to water, but not to solutes.

* Ascending limb: Impermeable to water but actively transports sodium chloride (NaCl) into the

surrounding tissue. *

This arrangement establishes a countercurrent system, where filtrate flows in opposite directions in the two
limbs of the loop. Simultaneously, blood in the vasa recta flows counter to-the flow in the nephron, helping
maintain the osmotic gradient.

Steps of the Countercurrent Multiplier Mechanism

1. Active NaCl Transport:
Sodium chloride is actively pumped out of the sscanaing limb into the medullary interstitium. This increases
the solute concentration in the surrounding tissue, making it hypertonic.

2. Water Reabsorption by Osmosis:
As filtrate flows down the descending limb, water moves out into the hypertonic interstitial fluid by osmosis,
concentrating the filtrate.
3. Flow Continuation and Exchange:

osmotic gradient in the medulla. As a result, about 99.5% of water is NCE TITBITS

KIDNEYS AS ORGANS OF EXCRETION AND OSMOREGULATION

The kidneys are vital organs of the urinary system that play a dual role in maintaining the body’s internal
balance. They function not only as excretory organs, removing waste products of metabolism, but also as
osmoregulatory organs, regulating the concentration of water and salts in body fluids. These two roles are closely
linked, as efficient excretion requires controlled regulation of fluid and electrolyte balance.

Kidneys as Excretory Organs :

Excretion is the process of removing metabolic wastes from the body. The kidneys filter blood through
specialized structures called nephrons, which separate useful substances from harmful wastes.
1. Removal of Nitrogenous Wastes:

¢ Proteins and nucleic acids are metabolized to produce nitrogenous wastes such as urea, creatinine, and

uric acid.

* These compounds are toxic if allowed to accumulate, so the kidneys filter them out and excrete them in

urine.
2. Detoxification of the Blood:

© Drugs, toxins, and by-products of metabolism (e.g., ammonia converted to urea in the liver) are

eliminated.

¢ This purification ensures that blood leaving the kidneys is free from harmful metabolic end products.
3. Acid-Base Balance:

¢ By excreting hydrogen ions (H*) and reabsorbing bicarbonate (HCOs*), kidneys maintain the blood pH

within a narrow range (around 7.35-7.45).

© Without this, metabolic acidosis or alkalosis could impair cellular functions.

Thus, the kidneys serve as highly efficient filters, protecting the body from toxic buildup and maintaining
chemical stability.

Kidneys as Osmoregulatory Organs
Osmoregulation refers to the control of water and salt balance in the body to ensure homeostasis. Kidneys
maintain the osmotic pressure of blood plasma and regulate extracellular fluid composition.
1. Regulation of Water Balance:
e Theantidiuretic hormone (ADH) increases the permeability of the collecting ducts, allowing more water
to be reabsorbed into the bloodstream during dehydration.
e  Inconditions of excess water intake, less ADH is secreted, resulting in dilute urine.
2. Regulation of Salt (Electrolyte) Balance:
e The kidneys control the levels of sodium, potassium, chloride, and calcium ions.

® The hormone aldosterone,. secreted by the adrenal cortex, promotes sodium reabsorption and
potassium excretion in the distal tubule, which also indirectly regulates water retention.

3. Maintenance of Blood Pressure and Volume:
© Specialized kidney cells release renin, which triggers the renin-angiotensin—aldosterone system (RAAS).
This pathway increases blood pressure by vasoconstriction and stimulating sodium and water
reabsorption.
e Inthis way, kidneys play a central role in long-term regulation of blood pressure.
> Integration of Excretion and Osmoregulation
The excretory and osmoregulatory functions of kidneys are interdependent. For example:
When waste products are excreted, water is also removed. The kidneys must regulate the amount of
water lost to prevent dehydration.
© Similarly, regulation of sodium ions not only maintains osmotic balance but also determines the volume
of urine produced and the concentration of wastes.
This dual role allows the kidneys to maintain homeostasis — a stable internal environment despite external
changes. For instance, during intense exercise, increased metabolic wastes (urea, lactic acid) must be
excreted, while at the same time water and electrolytes lost in sweat must be balanced by kidney regulation.

URINARY TRACT INFECTIONS (UTIS) AND THEIR CAUSATIVE BACTERIA

Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most frequent bacterial infections in humans, affecting millions
of people worldwide each year. The urinary system, which includes the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra, is
normally kept sterile by various defense mechanisms such as regular urination, mucosal barriers, and immune
responses. However, when bacteria gain entry and begin to multiply within this system, infection occurs. UTIs are
more common in women due to their shorter urethra and its close proximity to the anal opening, which facilitates
the transfer of bacteria.

From a medical perspective, UTIs can be classified according to the site of infection: urethritis (infection of
the urethra), cystitis (infection of the bladder), and pyelonephritis (infection of the kidneys). In some cases,
bacteria may be present in urine without obvious symptoms; this condition is called asymptomatic bacteriuria.
Each type of infection has distinct clinical significance and is caused by characteristic groups of bacteria.

1. Urethritis

Urethritis refers to the infection of the urethra, the narrow tube that carries urine from the bladder to the
outside. It often presents with painful urination (dysuria), itching, or discharge. While Escherichia coli (E.
coli), a common bacterium of the gut, can cause urethritis, two other important bacterial agents are sexually
transmitted: Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae. These pathogens are responsible for a
large proportion of sexually acquired urethral infections in young adults. If untreated, such infections may
spread to the reproductive tract, causing complications such as pelvic inflammatory disease in females or
infertility in males.

Cystitis

When the infection spreads upward from the urethra into the bladder, it leads to cystitis. This condition is
especially common in women and is characterized by urinary urgency, frequent urination in small amounts,
pain during urination, and cloudy or foul-smelling urine. The most common bacterium responsible is
Escherichia coli, which accounts for nearly 80-85% of all bladder infections. Another bacterium,
Staphylococcus saprophyticus, is frequently implicated in young, sexually active females. Less common
agents include Klebsiella pneumoniae and Proteus mirabilis, which are often associated with hospital-
acquired infections.

3. Pyelonephritis
{f the infection continues to ascend, it can reach the kidneys, causing pyelonephritis. This is a serious
condition marked by fever, chills, back pain (flank pain), and sometimes nausea or vomiting. Escherichia coli
remains the primary cause, but other bacteria such as Proteus mirabilis, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and
Pseudomonas aeruginosa are also involved, especially in patients with long-term catheters or structural
abnormalities of the urinary tract. Pyelonephritis can lead to permanent kidney damage if not treated

Types of Urinary Stones

Urinary stones, or renal calculi, are solid mineral and salt aggregates that form within the urinary tract. Based

© Calcium Oxalate Stones: These are the most common type, typically formed when urine contains high

© Calcium Phosphate Stones: These stones usually develop in alkaline urine and may be associated with

Explain in detail the mechanism and problems related to dialysis.

DIALYSIS: MECHANISM

Renal dialysis is a medical procedure used to remove toxins, excess water, and waste products from the
blood when the kidneys can no longer perform these vital functions adequately. Although dialysis mimics the
natural function of kidneys, it is comparatively less efficient and cannot entirely replicate their complex processes.
There are two primary types of dialysis: haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis.

Haemodialysis

Haemodialysis involves the removal of waste materials and excess fluids by circulating the patient’s blood
through an external filtration system known as a dialyzer. This system uses tubes made of semipermeable
membranes that allow the selective exchange of substances.

S$ studyplusplus.com S$

A catheter is inserted into a large blood vessel, usually in the arm, through which blood is withdrawn and
passed into the dialysis machine. The blood pump directs the blood into the dialyzer from the top. Inside the
dialyzer, blood flows through synthetic cellophane tubing, while a special fluid called dialysate flows around these
tubes in the opposite direction. The dialysate, which does not contain waste products, draws out urea, creatinine,
excess ions, and other metabolic wastes from the blood via diffusion across the semipermeable membrane.

Once filtered, the cleaned blood exits from the bottom of the machine and is returned to the patient's body
through a second catheter. The used dialysate exits from the top of the machine, carrying the filtered waste
materials with it.

Peritoneal Dialysis

Peritoneal dialysis utilizes the body's own peritoneal membrane—a natural semipermeable lining of the
abdominal cavity—as the filtration surface. In this method, two surgically placed catheters serve as channels for
the introduction and removal of dialysate.

During the process, dialysate is infused into the peritoneal cavity. As blood flows through the capillaries
lining the peritoneum, waste products and excess ions move across the membrane into the dialysate by diffusion
and osmosis. After a set dwell time, the fluid containing these wastes is drained out and replaced with fresh
dialysate. This exchange may be repeated several times a day, depending on the patient's clinical needs.

Problems and Complications Related to Dialysis

While dialysis is life-saving, it is not a perfect substitute for kidney function and is associated with several
challenges:

1. Medical Complications
e Infections: Hemodialysis access sites and peritoneal catheters are prone to infection. Peritoneal dialysis
may cause peritonitis, a serious abdominal infection.
e Hypotension: Rapid removal of fluid during hemodialysis can cause sudden drops in blood pressure.

e Electrolyte Imbalances: Incorrect dialysate composition may lead to dangerous levels of potassium,
sodium, or calcium.

¢ Anemia and Bone Disease: Dialysis cannot replace the kidney’s hormonal functions, such as producing
erythropoietin (for red blood-cells) or activating vitamin D. Patients often develop anemia and weak
bones.
2. Lifestyle Challenges
e Time-Consuming: Hemodialysis requires long sessions multiple times a week, interfering with work and
daily life.
e Dietary Restrictions: Patients must limit intake of fluids, salt, potassium, and phosphorus.
e Dependence on Machines: Dialysis cannot fully restore health; patients remain dependent on treatment
for survival unless they receive a kidney transplant.
3. Emotional and Financial Burden
e Dialysis treatment is costly and requires regular hospital visits.
© Long-term patients may experience psychological stress, depression, and reduced quality of life.
> Real-Life Relevance
In Pakistan and many other countries, thousands of patients rely on dialysis due to the rising incidence of
diabetes and hypertension, the two major causes of kidney failure. While dialysis prolongs life, it is not a
cure. Kidney transplantation remains the most effective long-term solution, but limited availability of donors
and high costs make dialysis the only option for many.

Advances in portable and home-based dialysis are improving quality of life, but prevention of kidney diseases
through healthy lifestyle, proper hydration, and early treatment of diabetes and hypertension remains the
best strategy. :

KIDNEY TRANSPLANT: PRINCIPLES AND ASSOCIATED PROBLEMS

When kidneys fail permanently and can no longer perform their vital functions of excretion and
osmoregulation, patients require artificial support through dialysis or surgical replacement of the kidney. Kidney
transplantation is the most effective long-term treatment for end-stage renal disease (ESRD). It involves surgically
placing a healthy kidney from a donor into a patient whose kidneys are no longer functioning. Unlike dialysis,
which only partially replaces kidney function, transplantation restores most natural kidney activities, including
hormone production, waste removal, and osmoregulation.

S$ studyplusplus.com S$

Principles of Kidney Transplant

Kidney transalantation is the most effective long-term treatment for patients suffering from end-stage renal
failure. However, the success of this procedure depends on several biological, medical, and surgical principles.
Understanding these principles helps explain why some transplants succeed for decades, while others fail within

a short time.

1. Donor-Recipient Matching
The most crucial factor in a successful kidney transplant is ensuring compatibility between the donor and
recipient.

Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) Matching: The HLA system is a group of proteins found’on the surface
of white blood cells and other tissues. They act like "biological ID cards" that help the immune system
distinguish between self and non-self. A closer HLA match between donor and recipient reduces the risk
of the body rejecting the transplanted kidney. For example, siblings often make better donors because
they share more HLA genes.

Blood Group Compatibility: Matching the ABO blood group system (A, B, AB, O) between donor and
recipient is equally important. A mismatch in blood type can trigger immediate rejection (hyperacute
rejection), making transplantation impossible.

Careful donor-recipient matching is therefore the foundation of transplant success.
Source of Donor Kidneys
Kidneys for transplantation can come from either living donors or deceased donors.

Living Donors: Often, close relatives such as parents, siblings, or even children donate a kidney. Living
donor kidneys are usually healthier and function more effectively after transplantation. They also allow
the surgery to be planned in advance, minimizing waiting time. Importantly, humans can live normally
with one kidney, making living donation safe in most cases.

Deceased Donors: These are individuals who have suffered brain death or cardiac death but whose
kidneys are still healthy. Such kidneys.can be transplanted if the individual consented to organ donation
during their lifetime, or if their family permits it after death. Deceased donor programs expand the pool
of available kidneys but outcomes may sometimes be slightly less favorable than with living donors.

In countries like Pakistan, deceased donor programs are limited, which adds to the shortage of kidneys and
prolongs patient waiting times.

Surgical Procedure

The surgical placement of a transplanted kidney follows specific principles to ensure both function and safety.

Placement of the Kidney: The new kidney is placed in the lower abdomen (iliac fossa), near the pelvis,
rather than in the original position of the natural kidneys. This location provides easier access to blood
vessels and the bladder.

Connection of Blood Vessels: The donor kidney’s renal artery and renal vein are surgically attached to
the recipient's iliac artery and iliac vein, ensuring proper blood flow.

Connection of the Ureter: The donor kidney’s ureter is connected directly to the recipient's bladder,
allowing urine to pass out normally.

Retention of Diseased Kidneys: In most cases, the patient's damaged kidneys are not removed. They
are left in place unless they cause complications such as recurrent infections, severe hypertension, or
kidney cancers.

This surgical strategy minimizes risks and ensures the transplanted kidney can function quickly after blood
flow is restored.

Immunosuppression

Since the transplanted kidney comes from another individual, the recipient’s immune system naturally
recognizes it as foreign. Without intervention, the immune system would attack the graft, leading to
rejection. To prevent this, patients must take immunosuppressive drugs for life.

Common Immunosuppressants: Drugs such as cyclosporine, tacrolimus, azathioprine, and
corticosteroids are given in combination. These reduce the activity of immune cells that would
otherwise damage the graft.

Balancing Risks: While these drugs are essential for graft survival, they also weaken the patient's
defense against infections and cancers. Doctors must carefully adjust doses to balance the risk of
rejection with the side effects of long-term immunosuppression.

Without immunosuppressive therapy, no kidney transplant could succeed.

Problems Associated with Kidney Transplant

Kidney transplantation is considered the gold standard treatment for end-stage renal failure because it

restores natural kidney function more effectively than dialysis. However, despite its advantages, it is not free from
challenges. Medical, surgical, and social complications can affect the success of the procedure and the patient's

. long-term survival. The following are the major problems associated with kidney transplantation:
1.

Organ Rejection

The immune system is designed to protect the body from foreign invaders..Unfortunately, a transplanted

kidney is also recognized as “foreign,” even if it comes from a close relative. This immune attack is known as

rejection.

e  Hyperacute Rejection: This occurs within minutes to hours after transplantation if the donor and
recipient tissues are poorly matched. The patient's antibodies attack the kidney immediately, causing
clotting within the blood vessels of the graft. Hyperacute rejection is rare today because careful tissue
and blood matching is done before surgery.

e Acute Rejection: This typically develops days to weeks after the operation. It is caused by the recipient's
immune cells (T lymphocytes) attacking the kidney tissue. Modern immunosuppressive drugs can often
reverse acute rejection if detected early.

@ Chronic Rejection: This is a slow, progressive rejection that occurs months or years after transplantation.
The blood vessels of the transplanted kidney gradually thicken and scar tissue forms, leading to a steady
decline in kidney function. Unlike acute rejection, chronic rejection is usually irreversible and is the
leading cause of long-term graft failure.

Even with strong immunosuppressive therapy, rejection remains the most serious complication of kidney

transplantation and requires lifelong monitoring.

Side Effects of Immunosuppressive Drugs

To prevent rejection, patients must take immunosuppressive drugs for life. While. these medicines: are

lifesaving, they also create new health challenges:

® Weak Immune Defense: Immunosuppressants reduce the body’s ability to fight infections. Patients are
more prone to bacterial, viral, and fungal infections, including pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and

shingles. Even minor infections can become life-threatening.

© Delayed Healing: Surgical wounds and minor injuries take longer to heal because of weakened immune
activity.

e Cancer Risk: Prolonged suppression of immunity increases the likelihood of certain cancers, especially
skin cancers and lymphomas.

Metabolic Side Effects: Drugs such as corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors may cause high blood
pressure, diabetes, osteoporosis (bone weakness), and excessive hair growth.

¢ Thus, while immunosuppressive drugs protect the graft, they also create a delicate balance between
preventing rejection and maintaining overall health.

Shortage of Donor Kidneys

The demand for kidney transplantation far exceeds the supply of donor organs worldwide.

¢ Long Waiting Lists: Thousands of patients remain dependent on dialysis for years, waiting for a
compatible kidney. In many countries, the waiting period can stretch from 3 to 7 years.

* Limited Donor Sources: Living donors (usually relatives) are more successful, but not always available.
Deceased donor programs exist, but cultural beliefs and lack of awareness about orga. donation often
limit participation.

e Ethical and Social Concerns: The shortage has led to unethical practices such as illegal organ trade and
exploitation of the poor, especially in developing countries. International guidelines now Promote strict
regulation of organ donation to prevent exploitation.

This shortage remains a major barrier to successful transplantation programs, particularly in countries like

Pakistan where awareness about cadaveric donation is still low.

Surgical and Medical Complications

As with any major surgery, kidney transplantation carries inherent risks, both during and after the procedure.

«Intraoperative Risks: Complications during surgery may include bleeding, blood clots, or injury to
surrounding structures. These are managed with careful surgical techniques and monitoring.

e Postoperative Infections: Surgical wounds and urinary tract infections are common due to
immunosuppression.

S$ studyplusplus.com S$

® Delayed Graft Function (DGF): In some cases, the transplanted kidney does not start working
immediately. The patient may need dialysis in the first few days or weeks until the new kidney recovers.

e Recurrence of Original Kidney Disease: In certain conditions (e.g., glomerulonephritis), the disease that
damaged the original kidneys can also affect the transplanted one.

Kidney transplantation has dramatically improved survival and quality of life for patients with ESRD. In

Pakistan and many other countries, however, limited availability of donors, high costs, and lack of awareness

about organ donation programs restrict access to this treatment. Patients often rely on living related donors,

which raises ethical and medical challenges.

Modern advances such as paired kidney exchange programs (where families swap donors for better

compatibility) and xenotransplantation research (using genetically modified animal organs) may help

address the shortage in the future.

Ans. The countercurrent multiplier mechanism occurs in the loop of Henle

The nervous system of man is a highly specialized and complex network that controls and coordinates all
activities of the body. It enables the body to sense changes in the internal and external environment and respond
to them appropriately, thereby maintaining balance and ensuring survival. The nervous system carries out three
essential roles: it detects stimuli through sense organs, processes and interprets the information in the brain and
spinal cord, and initiates suitable responses by stimulating muscles or glands. Structurally, it is divided into the
central nervous system, which includes the brain and spinal cord and is responsible for integration and control,
and the peripheral nervous system, which consists of nerves and ganglia and connects the central nervous system
with the rest of the body. In addition, the autonomic nervous system regulates involuntary activities such as
heartbeat, breathing, and digestion, thus ensuring the smooth functioning of vital organs. Altogether, the nervous
system serves as the body’s main control and communication center, making it possible for humans to think, learn,

RECEPTORS AS BIOLOGICAL TRANSDUCERS

What is a Transducer?

A transducer is any device that can convert energy from one form to another. In engineering, microphones
convert sound into electrical signals and solar panels convert light into electricity. Similarly, in biology, receptors
act as natural transducers that convertenvironmental energies — such as light, sound, temperature, pressure, or
chemicals — into electrochemical impulses that the nervous system can understand.
> Definition of Keceptor

A receptor is a cell, tissue, or organ capable of detecting a stimulus in the environment and converting it
into an electrical message (nerve impulse). These impulses are then carried by sensory neurons to the central
nervous system (CNS), where they are interpreted and transformed into appropriate responses.

> Types of Stimuli

Receptors can detect both internal stimuli (arising inside the body) and external stimuli (coming from the

surroundings).

© Internal Stimuli: Any change occurring inside the organism is called an internal stimulus. Examples
include hunger, thirst, fluctuations in blood pH, blood pressure, or the presence of pathogens such as
during a viral infection. Detecting such stimuli helps the body maintain homeostasis.

* External Stimuli: Any change in the external environment is called an external stimulus. Examples
include light, sound, heat, touch, and mechanical pressure. Detecting such stimuli allows the organism
to interact effectively with its environment and ensures survival,

> Structural Organization of Receptors

Receptors exist in two main forms:

1. Specialized Receptors in Sense Organs: These are highly organized and sensitive to specific stimuli. For
example, photoreceptors in the retina detect light, mechanoreceptors in the inner ear detect sound and
balance, and chemoreceptors in the nose and tongue detect smell and taste.

2. Receptors Dispersed in Body Tissues: These are scattered throughout the body, such as
mechanoreceptors and thermoreceptors in the skin (for touch, pain, and temperature) or baroreceptors
in blood vessels (for blood pressure regulation). They provide continuous feedback to maintain internal
balance.

> Examples of Major Receptor Types

* Photoreceptors: Detect light (e.g., rods and cones in the retina).

¢ Mechanoreceptors: Detect pressure, vibration, touch, and sound (e.g., skin receptors, ear hair cells).

* Thermoreceptors: Detect changes in temperature (e.g., in skin and hypothalamus).

« Chemoreceptors: Detect chemicals (e.g,, taste buds, olfactory cells, oxygen receptors in blood vessels).

* Nociceptors: Detect pain caused by harmful stimull (e.g., tissue damage).

Real-Life Applications and Impact

Receptors are not just biological structures — they are the reason humans and other organisms can survive,

adapt, and thrive.

© Driving a Car: Photoreceptors detect light signals, mechanoreceptors in muscles and joints sense
movement, and auditory receptors detect horns or sirens. Together, they allow safe and quick reactions.

© Medical Diagnostics: Understanding chemoreceptors has led to glucose sensors for diabetic patients
and pH monitoring devices for patients with acid-base imbalances.

Survival Instincts: Nociceptors alert the body to potential harm. For example, when touching a hot
object, thermoreceptors and nociceptors instantly send signals that trigger a withdrawal reflex before
conscious thought occurs.

® Homeostasis: Internal receptors such as baroreceptors and osmoreceptors continuously monitor blood
pressure and osmotic balance, ensuring stable internal conditions essential for life.

PATH OF A MESSAGE TO THE CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM

The central nervous system (CNS) cannot respond to the environment unless it receives information from

receptors. The journey of this information — called sensory transmission — begins at the receptor, travels along
sensory pathways, and ends in the brain, where it is interpreted. This organized flow ensures that the body can
detect, analyze, and respond effectively to both internal and external changes.

Transmission of Sensory Information: Neural Pathway to the Brain

Sensory perception begins with the detection of stimuli and progresses through a highly organized neural

pathway to reach the brain, where the information is interpreted. This pathway usually follows a three-neuron
relay system:

1.

First-Order Neuron (Sensory Neuron)

The first-order neuron is the initial component of the sensory pathway. It originates in peripheral tissues
such as the skin, muscles, joints, or internal organs and transmitsimpiilses to the CNS. These neurons detect
various stimuli including touch, pain, pressure, temperature, and body position (proprioception) through
specialized receptor cells.

The cell bodies of first-order neurons are found in dorsal root ganglia (for the body) or cranial nerve ganglia
(for the head region). Their axons synapse with second-order neurons in the spinal cord or brainstem.
Example: When you touch a sharp pin, receptors in the skin activate first-order sensory neurons, which carry
the impulse toward the spinal cord.

Second-Order Neuron (Interneuron)

The second-order neuron receives input from the first-order neuron. It is usually located in the dorsal horn
of the spinal cord or in the brainstem, depending on the pathway. Its main function is to relay and
sometimes integrate sensory input before forwarding it to higher brain centers.

In most pathways, the axons of second-order neurons decussate (cross over) to the opposite side of the CNS
and then ascend to the thalamus, which acts as the main relay station for sensory information. ~
Example: In pain perception, the second-order neuron in the spinal cord transmits the impulse to the
thalamus after crossing to the opposite side. This explains why the left side of the brain processes pain from
the right side of the body.

Third-Order Neuron ass
The third-order neuron resides in the thalamus and serves as the final relay in the ascending sensory
pathway. It projects axons to the primary somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe of the cerebrum

to your cerebral cortex, allowing you to consciously recognize the warmth.

MUSCLES AND GLANDS AS EFFECTORS

The nervous system not only detects and processes information but also produces a response to maintain
balance and ensure survival. This response is carried out by effectors — specialized structures that bring about an
action when stimulated by nerve impulses. In humans, the two main effectors are muscles and glands.

What are Effectors?

Effectors are organs or tissues that receive commands from the central nervolls system through motor
neurons and then carry out the required response. They serve as the final link in the pathway of information flow,
converting nerve impulses into visible actions such as movement, secretion, or regulation of body functions.

Muscles as Effectors

Muscles serve as the mechanical effectors of the nervous system. When stimulated by motor neurons, they
convert electrical impulses into mechanical action by contracting and generating force. This allows the body to
move, maintain posture, circulate blood, and regulate essential internal processes. Muscles are essential not only
for voluntary actions like walking or speaking but also for involuntary functions such as breathing, digestion, and
heartbeat.
> Types of Muscles as Effectors
1." Skeletal Muscles

¢ Structure and Control: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones via tendons and are under voluntary
control through the somatic nervous system. .

* Function: They are responsible for conscious actions such as walking, writing, speaking, and maintaining
body posture. They respond quickly but can fatigue easily.

« Example as Effector: When you accidentally touch a hot surface, the sensory message is relayed to the
spinal cord, and motor neurons activate skeletal muscles in your arm to withdraw the hand immediately
(reflex action).

¢ Application/impact: Skeletal muscles allow humans to interact with their environment. Disorders such
as muscular dystrophy weaken skeletal muscles, showing their vital role in everyday life.

2. Smooth Muscles
* Structure and Control: Smooth muscles are found in the walls of internal organs such as the stomach,
intestines, urinary bladder, and blood vessels. They are involuntary muscles controlled by the
autonomic nervous system.
* Function: They carry out slow, sustained actions like peristalsis in the digestive tract, constriction and
dilation of blood vessels, and regulation of airways in the lungs.
* Example as Effector: When blood pressure falls, smooth muscles in the blood vessels constrict to restore
normal circulation.
*  Application/Impact: Smooth muscle control is essential for homeostasis. Overconstriction of airway
smooth muscles, as in asthma, shows how malfunction can endanger life.
3. Cardiac Muscle
¢ Structure and Control: Found only in the heart, cardiac muscle fibers are striated but involuntary. They
have intrinsic pacemaker activity and are also regulated by the autonomic nervous system.
* Function: Cardiac muscle contracts rhythmically and continuously throughout life, pumping blood to
every part of the body, It is fatigue-resistant, ensuring uninterrupted circulation.
* Example as Effector: During exercise, sympathetic nerves stimulate cardiac muscle to increase heart
rate and stroke volume, delivering more oxygen and nutrients to muscles.
© Application/impact: Cardiac muscle is critical for survival. Conditions like arrhythmias or heart failure
demonstrate the importance of precise nervous and hormonal regulation of this effector.
> Integration of Muscles as Effectors
Muscles act as the final executors of motor commands from the nervous system. For instance, in the simple
act of running:
* Skeletal muscles move the limbs,
* Smooth muscles in blood vessels adjust blood flow, and
® Cardiac muscle increases output to meet oxygen demand.
This shows how all three muscle types coordinate as effectors to carry out complex body responses.
Glands as Effectors

Glands are specialized structures in the body that produce and secrete substances essential for regulation,

coordination, and survival. Unlike muscles, which bring about movement, glands act as chemical effectors. They
release their secretions either into ducts or directly into the bloodstream, influencing processes such as digestion,
temperature regulation, stress response, metabolism, and reproduction. Glands may be stimulated by nerve
impulses (neurogenic control) or by chemical messengers (hormonal feedback).

1.

Exocrine Glands
Exocrine glands discharge their secretions into ducts that open either onto the body surface or into body
cavities. These secretions perform local and immediate actions.
« Examples and Roles: [ :
© Salivary glands: Secrete saliva into the oral cavity, moistening food and initiating starch digestion
through the enzyme amylase.
o Sweat glands: Release sweat onto the skin surface, playing a vital role in cooling the body during
exercise or heat stress. : g
© Gastric glands: Secrete digestive juices containing hydrochloric acid and pepsin, aiding in protein
digestion.
© Sebaceous glands; Secrete sebum, an oily substance that lubricates and protects the skin and hair.
* Application and Impact: Exocrine gland function is crucial for everyday life. For example, reduced saliva
secretion (xerostomia) can lead to difficulty in chewing and swallowing, while blocked sweat glands can
cause overheating of the body.

2. Endocrine Glands

Endocrine glands are ductless glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream. Unlike exocrine

secretions, hormones act on distant target organs and regulate long-term and wide-ranging processes.

* Examples and Roles:

o Adrenal glands: Secrete adrenaline (epinephrine) during stress, preparing the body for “fight or
flight” by increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and glucose availability.

© Pancreas (Islets of Langerhans): Secretes insulin and glucagon, hormones essential for regulating
blood glucose levels.

o Thyroid gland: Produces thyroxine, which regulates metabolism, growth, and energy balance.

© Pituitary gland: Known as the “master gland,” it secretes hormones that control other endocrine
glands and regulate growth, reproduction, and water balance. .

¢ Application and Impact: Endocrine control is vital for maintaining homeostasis. For instance, a deficiency

of insulin leads to diabetes mellitus, while overproduction of thyroxine causes hyperthyroidism. Medical

treatment often involves replacing or regulating these hormones to restore balance.

Together, exocrine and endocrine glands ensure the body's adaptation to both internal and external
demands. For example, when running on a hot day, sweat glands (exocrine) release sweat to cool the body, while
adrenal glands (endocrine) secrete adrenaline to increase stamina and prepare muscles for exertion. This shows
how glands function as chemical executors of the nervous system’s commands.

> Real-Life Applications and Impact

* Muscle Effectors in Reflexes: When stepping ona sharp object, receptors in the skin detect pain, sensory
neurons carry the message to the spinal cord, and motor neurons activate leg muscles to withdraw the
foot instantly.

* Gland Effectors in Stress; When facing danger, the hypothalamus signals the adrenal glands to release
adrenaline. This causes increased heart rate, faster breathing, and energy mobilization — preparing the
body for “fight or flight.”

* Medical Relevance: Diseases such'as myasthenia gravis (affecting skeletal muscle response) or diabetes
mellitus (due to insulin deficiency from pancreatic glands) show the critical role of effectors in
maintaining normal physiology.

* Everyday Example: Sweating while running on a hot day involves both muscles (increased heart and
breathing rates) and glands (sweat secretion) working together to protect the body.

Effectors are the organs that execute the commands of the nervous system, Muscles respond by contracting

and causing movement, while glands respond by secreting essential substances. Together, they ensure that the
body can interact with the environment, maintain internal balance, and survive under varying conditions.

DETAILED STRUCTURE OF SENSORY, ASSOCIATIVE AND MOTOR NEURONS

Although neurons vary in their size and shape, they all share the same fundamental plan: a cell body (soma)
with a nucleus and Niss! bodies, dendrites that receive information, and an axon that conducts impulses to another
cell. Within this general plan, sensory neurons, associative (interneurons), and motor neurons each show distinct
structural features that enable them to perform their specialized functions. The following sections describe their
detailed structures, as required for annotation and examination.

Sensory Neurons (Afferent Neurons)

Sensory neurons are responsible for transmitting information from receptors in the skin, muscles, joints, and
internal organs to the central nervous system (CNS). Most vertebrate sensory neurons are pseudounipolar, a
design well suited for rapid conduction.

The cell body of a sensory neuron Is located in the dorsal root ganglion of spinal nerves or in the sensory
ganglia of cranial nerves. This soma is typically round, with a large nucleus and a prominent nucleolus, and is
encircled by satellite glial cells. A key feature of these ganglion cells is that they do not receive synapses directly

on their soma.

From the cell body arises a single process, which quickly bifurcates in a T-shaped fashion into two branches:

* the peripheral process, which extends to a sensory receptor such as a free nerve ending, a pressure

corpuscle, or a muscle spindle,

© and the central process, which enters the spinal cord through the dorsal root and terminates in the

dorsal horn.

Both branches are structurally axons and are usually myelinated, with nodes of Ranvier at regular intervals
to allow saltatory conduction. This arrangement permits impulses to travel rapidly and with minimal delay from
the receptor to the CNS.

Thus, sensory neurons are highly specialized for uninterrupted transmission of impulses from the body's
periphery to the spinal cord and brain.

Associative Neurons (interneurons)

interneurons, also called relay neurons or association neurons, are located entirely within the CNS. They
form the largest class of neurons and are essential for the integration, processing, and relay of information

Structurally, interneurons are usually multipolar, with a relatively small cell body containing abundant Niss!

synapses locally within the grey matter of the brainor spinal cord.

This dense network of dendrites and short axons enables interneurons to establish thousands of synaptic
connections. Their structural plan perfectly matches thelr role in reflex arcs, local circuit activity, and higher brain
functions such as memory, learning, and decision-making.

In summary, interneurons are designed for integration and coordination rather than long-distance
transmission.

RELATING THE STRUCTURE OF NEURONS WITH THEIR FUNCTIONS

Neurons are specialized cells whose structures are perfectly adapted to their functions in the nervous

system. Each part of a neuron—cell body, dendrites, axon, and synaptic terminals—plays a distinct role in
receiving, processing, and transmitting information, The efficiency of the nervous system depends on this precise
relationship between structure and function.

Cell Body (Soma or Perikaryon)

The cell body serves as the metabolic and synthetic center of the neuron. It contains a large nucleus with a
prominent nucleolus, indicating high levels of gene activity. The cytoplasm, also called neuroplasm, Is rich in Niss!
bodies (aggregations of rough endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes), which produce structural proteins and
neurotransmitters required for signal transmission.

Other organelles, such as numerous mitochondria, provide the ATP needed for ion pumping, axonal
transport, and synaptic activity. The Golgi apparatus packages proteins into vesicles for delivery to axon terminals.
A robust cytoskeleton (microtubules, actin filaments, and neurofilaments) maintains the shape of the cell and
forms tracks for axonal transport. Together, these features ensure that the soma supports the enormous
metabolic demands of the neuron and sustains long-distance communication.

Dendrites: The Receiving Structures

Dendrites are short, tapering, and highly branched extensions that provide a large surface area for synaptic
input. Many dendrites bear dendritic spines, which are small projections packed with postsynaptic receptors and
signaling molecules, These spines are sites of synaptic plasticity, meaning their structure changes during
processes like learning and memory.

Dendrites act as the receptive region of the neuron, They receive signals from thousands of presynaptic
terminals, and their branching pattern allows spatial and temporal summation of incoming impulses. In this way,
dendrites filter and integrate information before it reaches the cell body and axon hillock.

Axon: The Conducting Structure

Each neuron has a single axon, which conducts impulses away from the cell body. The axon arises from a
specialized region called the axon hillock, and its adjacent Initial segment is rich in voltage-gated sodium
channels, making it the trigger zone for action potential initiation.

The diameter of the axon strongly influences conduction speed; larger diameters reduce resistance and
conduct impulses faster. Within the axon, bundles of microtubules and neurofilaments serve as tracks for
anterograde transport (moving vesicles and organelles from the soma to terminals via kinesin) and retrograde
transport (carrying signals and waste back to the soma via.dynein).

Myelination and Saltatory Conduction

Many axons are covered by a myelin sheath, formed by Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system
(PNS) or by oligodendrocytes in the central nervous system (CNS). Myelin acts as an insulating layer, interrupted
at intervals by Nodes of Ranvier, where the axonal membrane is exposed,

This arrangement allows saltatory conduction, in which action potentials “jump” from one node to the next,
greatly increasing the speed and energy efficiency of impulse transmission. Myelinated axons make up the white
matter of the nervous system, while non-myelinated axons conduct impulses more slowly by continuous
conduction and are common in the autonomic system.

Axon Terminals (Synaptic Boutons)

At its end, the axon branches into numerous axon terminals (or synaptic boutons), Each terminal contains
synaptic vesicles, mitochondria, and specialized proteins for neurotransmitter release. When an action potential
arrives, voltage-gated calclum channels open, triggering the fusion of vesicles with the presynaptic membrane.
Neurotransmitters are then released into the synaptic cleft, allowing the conversion of an electrical signal into a
chemical signal.

Synapses: The Communication Points
Neurons communicate at specialized junctions called synapses, Most are chemical synapses, which consist
of a presynaptic terminal, a synaptic cleft, and a postsynaptic membrane rich in receptors. These synapses allow
unidirectional, modifiable, and amplifiable transmission, essential for processes such as learning and memory.
In contrast, electrical synapses (formed by gap junctions) allow direct cytoplasmic continulty between
neurons. They enable fast and often bidirectional transmission, useful for synchronization of neuronal activity.

functional unit of the nervous system. Unlike most other cells, neurons
are excitable and can generate electrical impulses called action
potentials, Each neuron has the unique ability to receive, integrate, and
transmit information in the form of electrical and chemical signals, Neurons form complex communication
networks that coordinate voluntary actions, such as muscle movement, and involuntary processes, such as
breathing and heartbeat. Their primary role is to ensure rapid communication between different parts of

Q.1 How Is the structure of motor neurons sulted to their function?

‘Ans. Motor neurons, also called efferent neurons, are structurally adapted

to carry signals from the central nervous system to effectors like
muscles and glands. They are multipolar, possessing a single long axon

peripheral effectors. The axon terminals form neuromuscular junctions, releasing neurotransmitters that
trigger muscle contraction or glandular secretion. This structural design—large dendritic branching,
myelination, and long axonal projections—makes motor neurons perfectly suited for rapid, efficient, and
coordinated transmission of commands to initiate movement or physiological responses.

Q.4 Compare the conduction speed between myelinated and non-myelinated neurons.

Ans. The conduction speed of nerve impulses depends on whether an axon

NERVE IMPULSE

A nerve impulse is the electrical signal that travels along the length of a neuron. It is generated when a
neuron is stimulated by a change in the environment (stimulus) and represents the way information is transmitted
within the nervous system. In simple terms, it is the rapid movement of an electrical disturbance across the
neuron’s membrane, allowing messages to be carried from one part of the body to another.

Q.2 How do ion concentrations differ across the membrane during the resting state?
Ans. During the resting state, the ionic composition of the intracellular and

extracellular fluids differs significantly, producing the resting | . y+ — copii seg fa
membrane potential. Inside the neuron, potassium ions (K*) are present concentration (1.5).

in high concentration, around 140 mM, compared to much lower levels

outside. This abundance of K* within the cell allows outward diffusion through leaky potassium channels.
Conversely, sodium ions (Na*) are concentrated outside the neuron at about 145 mM, whereas their
concentration inside is much lower, approximately 15 mM. This steep sodium gradient favors the inward
flow of Na* whenever sodium channels open. The imbalance of these ion distributions, established and
maintained by the sodium—potassium pump, ensures the negative resting potential. This separation of
charges across the membrane is the basis of neuronal excitability.

Hyperpolarization creates a refractory period, during which the neuron is less likely to fire another action

Q.6 What Is the importance of the refractory period in nerve impulse transmission?
Ans. The refractory period Is the short interval following an action potential
during which a neuron cannot immediately fire another impulse. It has
two phases: the absolute refractory period, where no stimulus can
trigger another action potential because sodium channels are
inactivated, and the relative refractory period, where only a stronger-than-usual stimulus can initiate firing
due to ongoing potassium efflux, This mechanism Is critical for two reasons. First, it ensures unidirectional
propagation of impulses along the axon by preventing action potentials from moving backward. Second, it
provides time for the sodium-potassium pump to restore ionic gradients, reestablishing the resting

membrane potential. Without this period, signals could overlap, leading to chaotic or ineffective nerve
transmission.

VELOCITIES OF NERVE IMPULSE IN AXON MEMBRANE AND SYNAPTIC CLEFT

The conduction of a nerve impulse occurs in two distinct ways:
1. Along the axon membrane (intra-neuronal conduction).
2. Across the synaptic cleft (inter-neuronal transmission).
These processes differ significantly in speed, mechanism, and efficiency, mainly due to the structural and

physiological features of neurons.

Conduction along the Axon Membrane

The movement of a nerve impulse along the axon depends on ionic changes across the axon membrane.
Several factors influence its velocity:

1. Myelin Sheath and Saltatory Conduction

* In non-myelinated axons, impulses move continuously along the membrane, with a relatively slow
speed of 1-3 m/s.
In myelinated axons, the myelin sheath acts as an insulator and prevents ion leakage.
Here, impulses "jump" from one node of Ranvier to the next, in a process called saltatory conduction.
This mode of transmission is up to 50 times faster than conduction in non-myelinated fibres.
In humans, myelinated axons can transmit impulses at speeds up to 120 m/s, making them rapid and
energy-efficient.
2. Axon Diameter

© The thicker the axon, the faster the conduction.

© Larger diameters reduce internal resistance to the flow of ions, thereby increasing velocity.

© This principle isbased on the inverse relationship between resistance and the cross-sectional area of a conductor.
3. Energy Efficiency

* Myelinated axons Conserve energy because only the nodes of Ranvier require active ion exchange.
* This reduces metabolic cost while still maintaining high transmission speed.

Transmission across the Synaptic Cleft

When an impulse reaches the end of the axon (axon terminal), conduction switches from electrical to
chemical transmission: .
* The arrival of the action potential triggers the release of neurotransmitters (e.g., acetylcholine) into the
synaptic cleft.
* These neurotransmitters diffuse across the cleft (20-40-nm wide) and bind to specific receptors on the
postsynaptic membrane.
© This initiates a new action potential in the postsynaptic neuron.

Synaptic Delay

Transmission across the synapse introduces a délay of approximately 0.5—-1.0 milliseconds, called the
synaptic delay.
* This delay is due to the time required for:
© Release of neurotransmitters,
© Diffusion across the cleft,
© Binding to receptors,
© Activation of ion channels in the postsynaptic neuron.
* Although short, the synaptic delay is still longer than the time needed for the impulse to travel the same
distance along an axon.

ROLE OF LOCAL CIRCUITS IN SALTATORY CONDUCTION

Saltatory Conduction

In myelinated axons, nerve impulses are transmitted by a special process called saltatory conduction. in
this mode, the action potential does not travel continuously along every part of the axon membrane. Instead, it
appears to “jump” from one node of Ranvier to the next, bypassing the myelinated regions. This adaptation
makes conduction both much faster and more energy-efficient compared to unmyelinated fibres.

Mechanism: Local Circuits of lonic Current
The key mechanism underlying saltatory conduction is the formation of local circuits within the axon:

At an active node of Ranvier, voltage-gated sodium channels open, allowing a rapid influx of Na* ions,
which depolarizes that region.

These sodium ions spread longitudinally inside the axoplasm, creating a local circuit of current that
flows from thedepolarized node toward the adjacent resting node.

When this current reaches the next node, where sodium channels are densely concentrated, it
depolarizes the membrane to threshold potential.

A new action potential is then generated at that node, while the previous one enters its refractory
phase, ensuring forward movement only.

Thus, the impulse does not regenerate along the entire length of the axonal membrane, but is renewed
only at the nodes, giving the appearance of “jumping.”

Significance of Local Circuits

Local circuits make saltatory conduction possible and provide several advantages:

Rapid transmission: The action potential leaps between nodes, greatly accelerating the speed of
conduction (up to 120 m/s in humans).

Energy efficiency: Only nodal regions undergo depolarization, so fewer ions cross the membrane and
the Na*/K* pump expends less ATP.

Directional propagation: The refractory period behind each impulse prevents backward spread,
ensuring unidirectional flow of nerve signals. .

STRUCTURE OF A SYNAPSE

A synapse is the specialized junction between two neurons, or between a neuron and an effector (muscle
or gland). It serves as the site where nerve impulses are transmitted from one cell to another. Synapses ensure
that communication within the nervous system is highly organized and directional.

Major Components of a Synapse
1. Presynaptic Neuron

© The neuron that sends the message.

© Its terminal end (synaptic. knob or bouton) contains numerous synaptic vesicles filled with

neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine, dopamine, or norepinephrine.

© Italso contains mitochondria to supply ATP required for neurotransmitter release.

2. Synaptic Cleft

© Anarrow gap (~20=40;nanometers wide) that separates the presynaptic terminal from the postsynaptic

membrane.

« The nerve impulse cannot cross this gap electrically; instead, neurotransmitters diffuse across the cleft

to carry the signal chemically.
3.  Postsynaptic Membrane
* Located on the dendrite, soma, oreffector surface of the next cell.
* It contains specific receptor proteins that bind neurotransmitters.

* This binding generates a new electrical’signal in the postsynaptic neuron or triggers a response in an
effector cell (e.g., muscle contraction).

SYNAPTIC TRANSMISSION OF NERVE IMPULSE

The synapse is not just a structural junction but a functional site where the nerve impulse is transmitted
from one neuron to another, or from a neuron to an effector cell. This process, called synaptic transmission,
converts an electrical signal (action potential) in the presynaptic neuron into a chemical signal in the synaptic cleft,
and then back into an electrical response in the postsynaptic cell.

Sequence of Synaptic Transmission:

1. Arrival of Action Potential: When an action potential reaches the synaptic knob of the presynaptic neuron,
it triggers the opening of voltage-gated calcium channels in the presynaptic membrane.

2. _ Influx of Calcium Ions: Due to a steep concentration gradient, Ca** lons enter the synaptic knob, increasing
intracellular calcium levels.

3. Vesicle Fusion and Neurotransmitter Release: Elevated calcium concentration stimulates synaptic vesicles
to migrate and fuse with the presynaptic membrane. As a result, neurotransmitters are released into the
synaptic cleft via exocytosis.

4. _ Diffusion and Receptor Binding: Neurotransmitter molecules diffuse across the synaptic cleft and bind to
specific receptors on the postsynaptic membrane.

5. Generation of Postsynaptic Potential: Binding of neurotransmitters causes lon channels (e.g., Na* channels)
to open, allowing the influx of sodium Ions. This depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane and may initiate a
new action potential. If this depolarization is sufficient to reach the threshold, it is termed an Excitatory
Postsynaptic Potential (EPSP).

¢ Adrenaline (epinephrine) is degraded by monoamine oxidase (MAO).

CLASSIFICATIONS OF NEUROTRANSMITTERS
—
Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers that mediate communication between neurons or between
neurons and effectors across synapses. Depending on their action on the postsynaptic membrane, they are
classified as excitatory or inhibitory.

’ Excitatory Neurotransmitters
Excitatory neurotransmitters increase the likelihood of generating an action potential in the postsynaptic
neuron. They achieve this by enhancing the membrane’s permeability to sodium ions (Na*), thereby depolarizing
the membrane and bringing it closer to the threshold potential.
A prominent example is acetylcholine (ACh), which acts as a key excitatory neurotransmitter in the
peripheral nervous system, particularly at neuromuscular junctions. In the central nervous system (CNS), several
biogenic amines (derived from amino acids) serve excitatory roles.
